content.title: UNVEILING TRACHEAL STENOSIS: A STIFF PERSON SYNDROME SAGA
content.text: SESSION TITLE: Pulmonary Manifestations Case Reports Posters (Q)SESSION TYPE: Case Report PostersPRESENTED ON: 10/09/2024 12:30 pm - 01:15 pmINTRODUCTION: Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is a rare neurological disorder affecting one to two persons per million. The pathogenesis is believed to involve autoimmune mechanisms targeting GABA activity in the central nervous system. It is commonly characterized by debilitating muscle stiffness and spasms involving the axial and limb muscles. Exacerbations rarely manifest with respiratory failure requiring airway protection. The need for recurrent intubations is even rarer and poses a significant clinical challenge. We present a case illustrating the emergence of tracheal stenosis as a complication of SPS exacerbations.CASE PRESENTATION: A 54 year-old-female with SPS, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, and Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy presented with progressively stiff extremities and dyspnea for a few days. Patient was brought to the hospital on bag mask ventilation due to a drop in respiratory rate to 4 breaths/min. Physical exam was notable for a GCS of 6/15 with stiff and contracted extremities reflective of impending respiratory failure and necessitating rapid sequence intubation. Further history was significant for prior hospitalizations with similar presentations. Infectious work-up including respiratory viral panel, streptococcal and legionella antigen, urine and blood cultures were negative. Chest X-ray was unremarkable. The patient was treated with benzodiazepines, tizanidine, gabapentin, and valproate. She was successfully extubated to 2 L nasal cannula on day 2 of admission. Within 4 days of extubation, she was re-intubated after developing a new stridor with increased work of breathing. She was noted to have swelling of anterior oropharynx causing difficult airway intubation. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest revealed tracheal narrowing at the thoracic inlet confirming tracheal stenosis. Following treatment with steroids, antiepileptics, and muscle relaxants, she was successfully weaned from mechanical ventilation and discharged home after 12 days of hospitalization.DISCUSSION: The disease course of SPS is highly variable, ranging from slow progression to frequent acute exacerbations. Management primarily focuses on symptom control using GABA-enhancing, antispastic, and immunomodulatory therapies to improve overall mobility. Exacerbations involving acute respiratory failure are reported in only a handful of cases. Crescimanno et al. (2020) postulates abnormal activation of laryngeal constrictors and paroxysmal autonomic hyperactivity as possible mechanisms for respiratory crises. Our case developed tracheal stenosis secondary to recurrent intubations pursued during SPS exacerbations, revealing a previously undocumented aspect of the syndrome. Cai et al. (2020) reports that 10% of SPS patients experience sudden deaths, with respiratory failure and apnea as the cause in most cases. Our patient emphasizes the importance of vigilant respiratory monitoring in SPS and provides further understanding of disease progression.CONCLUSIONS: Our patient developed tracheal stenosis as a rare complication of SPS. We present this case to improve our understanding of the clinical manifestations of SPS, and to emphasize a need for further research into the disease course to allow for timely management.REFERENCE #1: 1.
